report:
## Conclusion

Your skepticism is well supported: the claim that prolonged cloth or surgical mask use causes dangerous CO2 buildup is false, according to the best available evidence.

**What the data show:**
Multiple direct physiological studies find that any CO2 increase under masks is small and physiologically insignificant. A 2021 study of healthcare workers wearing surgical and N95 masks for extended periods found CO2 levels rose slightly but "remained below" thresholds considered occupationally hazardous, with no signs of hypercapnia (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12879-021-06056-0). A JAMA Network Open study measuring end-tidal CO2, oxygen saturation, and respiratory rate in infants and young children wearing surgical masks found no clinically meaningful changes in respiratory function (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2776928). A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of N95 and surgical mask CO2 effects across activity levels similarly concluded that while masks produce measurable but modest CO2 increases, these do not reach dangerous or toxic levels for healthy wearers (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11386028/).

**Fact-checks and public health bodies:** Reuters, PolitiFact, and USA Today fact-checking teams reviewed viral claims of mask-induced hypercapnia/hypoxia and rated them false or misleading, citing CDC statements that CO2 buildup under masks is "mostly tolerable" and "unlikely to cause hypercapnia" (https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2020/dec/03/facebook-posts/masks-do-not-kill-people-and-do-not-reduce-blood-o/).

**Caveat:** Cloth and surgical masks are porous enough that CO2 diffuses out; effects may differ slightly for people with severe pre-existing lung disease, but no evidence supports "dangerous" buildup in the general population.
